---

Stretched and still lies the midnight, two great hulls lying motionless upon the breast of the darkness; our vessel, riddled through, sinks slowly, while preparations are made to pass across to the one we have conquered. The captain, upon the quarter-deck, coldly issues his orders through a countenance white as a sheet; nearby rests the corpse of the child who served in the cabin, and the lifeless face of an old salt, his long white hair and carefully curled whiskers still in place. The flames, in spite of all that can be done, flicker aloft and below, and the husky voices of the two or three officers yet fit for duty carry through the gloom. Formless stacks of bodies, and bodies lying by themselves, with dabs of flesh clinging upon the masts and spars; the cut of cordage, the dangle of rigging, the slight shock of the soothing waves. Black and impassive stand the guns, amid the litter of powder-parcels and a strong, pervading scent. A few large stars shine overhead, silent and mournful in their glow; delicate sniffs of the sea-breeze drift in, bearing the smells of sedgy grass and fields along the shore, while death-messages are given in charge to the survivors. The hiss of the surgeon's knife, the gnawing teeth of his saw, the wheeze, the cluck, the swash of falling blood, the short wild scream, and the long, dull, tapering groan—these, so it is; these, irretrievable.

---

outputs.L2:
The midnight hours drag on in eerie calm, two enormous ship hulls sitting frozen upon the dark water's surface. Our own craft, punctured through and gradually going under, as we ready ourselves to board the ship we've defeated. On the quarter-deck stands the captain, delivering commands with icy composure, his face drained of all color like bleached linen. Beside him rests the body of the young boy who worked the cabin, and the lifeless features of an aged sailor whose long white hair frames meticulously curled whiskers. Despite every effort to control them, fires still dance both high in the masts and down below. The rough, worn-out voices belong to the handful of officers still able to serve.

Bodies pile up in shapeless heaps, while others lie scattered alone; scraps of torn flesh cling to the masts and wooden beams. Ropes hang severed, the rigging sways loose, and the gentle rocking of the waves sends faint tremors through everything. The cannons sit dark and unmoved amid scattered packets of gunpowder, a powerful odor filling the air. Above, a scattering of bright stars glows down in quiet sorrow. Faint breaths of ocean wind carry the scent of marshy grasses and coastal meadows, while dying men entrust their final words to those who will live on. The surgeon's blade whispers as it cuts, his saw grinding through with hungry teeth. Blood spills with a wheeze, a gurgle, a splash; a brief, frantic cry pierces the air, followed by a drawn-out, hollow moan that slowly fades. All of this happened—all of it beyond any hope of undoing.
outputs.L3:
# The Aftermath of Battle

At the stroke of midnight, an unnatural stillness settled over the water where, only moments before, the fury of battle had raged. Two ships lay motionless upon the dark sea, their silhouettes stark against the night, while the narrator's own vessel—triumphant yet mortally wounded—began its slow and inevitable descent beneath the waves. Victory, it seemed, had come at a terrible price.

Amid the wreckage stood the captain, his face drained of all color, pale as a bleached sheet. With a coldness that belied the carnage around him, he issued his orders in measured tones, seemingly unmoved by the dead who lay scattered at his feet. Among the fallen were the most innocent and the most venerable alike—a young boy who had served as cabin servant, his small form now still, and an old sailor whose years of service had ended here upon these blood-soaked planks.

Throughout the dying ship, flames continued to flicker and dance, licking uncontrollably at the timber and rigging, casting their restless glow across the scene of devastation. The few officers who had survived the engagement strained their voices—now hoarse and husky from shouting through the chaos of combat—as they labored to maintain some semblance of order amid the ruin.

The deck itself had become a tableau of horror. Dismembered bodies and torn, bloody flesh lay strewn among the shattered debris of war, a grotesque testament to the violence that had unfolded. Yet, in cruel contrast to this butchery, nature offered its serene indifference: the stars shone calmly overhead, gentle sea-breezes drifted across the water, and the distant scents of the shore carried on the air, as though the world beyond remained untouched by such suffering.

The full weight of the horror reached its peak in sound as much as sight—the sickening rasp of the surgeon's saw performing its grim work of amputation, and the anguished cries of dying men echoing into the night. These were losses that could never be undone, wounds that no victory could heal, and lives that were now gone beyond all recovery—permanent, irretrievable, and final.
outputs.L4:
# The Aftermath of Battle

Midnight descends upon the wreckage of two vessels, locked together in the terrible embrace of naval combat now ended. The scene emerges through Whitman's unflinching eye—a tableau of destruction rendered in language that refuses to look away from war's true face.

The narrator surveys the devastation surrounding him. Both ships lie crippled, their once-proud forms reduced to broken hulls barely afloat upon the dark waters. His own vessel, wounded beyond saving, begins its slow descent into the depths. There is no glory here, no triumphant flourish of victory—only the mechanical certainty of a ship taking on water, sinking degree by inevitable degree.

Across the decks, the dead lie scattered where they fell. The corpses spread in disarray, and among them the wounded groan and struggle, their suffering laid bare without romantic embellishment. Whitman catalogs this horror with deliberate thoroughness—the blood, the mangled bodies, the raw physical reality of men torn apart by violence. He spares his reader nothing, insisting that we witness the full weight of what has occurred.

Yet even amid this carnage, moments of natural beauty intrude. Perhaps the stars wheel silently overhead, or the sea moves with its ancient indifference, or the night air carries some fleeting sweetness. These glimpses of the natural world's ongoing loveliness create a haunting contrast, sharpening rather than softening the surrounding horror. Beauty persists, unmoved and uncomprehending, while men die below.

Through this stark juxtaposition, the passage achieves its devastating power. Whitman conveys the irretrievable human cost of warfare—lives extinguished that cannot be reclaimed, suffering that serves no redemptive purpose. The permanence of this devastation stands at the heart of his vision. What war destroys stays destroyed. The men who fall will not rise again, and no cause, however righteous, can undo the finality of their loss.

In refusing to sentimentalize or glorify, Whitman offers instead an honest reckoning with war's essential nature: its indifference to human life, its transformation of living men into scattered dead, and the stark, unalterable truth of its aftermath.

Every morning, my partner and I begin our day with the same simple ritual. Before the sun fully rises, the **two** of us roll out our mats side by side and take a moment to **stretch** away the stiffness of sleep. It has become one of **our** most cherished habits.

There is something powerful about sharing this quiet time. As we reach toward the ceiling and lengthen our tired muscles, we also **stretch** our patience, our understanding, and our commitment to one another. The physical movement mirrors something deeper in **our** relationship—the constant effort to grow, to bend without breaking, and to support each other through every challenge.

When the **two** of us started this practice, we could barely touch our toes. Now, months later, we have both improved dramatically. But more than flexibility, we have gained a rhythm that belongs only to us. It is **our** time, protected from the noise of the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Walt Whitman-style free verse poem depicting the aftermath of a naval battle at night, focusing on the sinking ship, the dead, and vivid sensory details.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wreck at Midnight**

O the battle is done, and the guns lie cooling in their iron throats,
And I walk the sloping deck, I, the witness, the tallier of the dead,
Amid the smoke that will not lift, the acrid breath of powder settling low upon the waters.

Hear the ship, she groans, she settles, she takes the black brine into her ribs,
The great beams shudder and split, the timbers cry out like living things,
And down she leans, slow, patient, toward the fathomless bed prepared for her.

Look here—the lantern swings, and by its guttering yellow I see them:
The young sailor face-down in the scuppers, his hand still curled as if to grasp a rope,
The gunner slumped against his silent iron, cheek blackened, eyes wide to the indifferent stars,
The boy, the powder-monkey, no more than a child, laid quiet where he fell.

I do not turn away. I stoop, I look, I lay my palm upon the cold brows.
The moon comes ragged through the torn rigging, silvering the blood that pools and creeps,
The salt wind carries the smell of tar, of scorched wood, of the sweet-sick reek of wounds,
And under all, the ceaseless washing, wash, wash, of the sea against the broken hull.

Somewhere a wounded man is calling, calling on his mother in the dark,
Somewhere the water gurgles up through the shattered planking, a low and greedy music,
And the splintered mast, snapped like a matchstick, trails its canvas shroud upon the deep.

I hear the last cry and the no-cry, the silence heavier than any sound.
Comrades, sleepers, you who were living an hour ago, laughing, cursing, breathing—
Now you drift toward the wet and final darkness, and I go with you a little way in spirit.

The ship sighs, dips her prow, the sea closes green and cold above the wreck,
The bubbles rise, the flotsam scatters, a cap, a plank, a drifting oar,
And the stars look down, ancient, uncounting, upon the little tragedy of men.

I stand, I do not weep, I absorb it all into myself—
The dead, the ship, the smoke, the moon, the salt, the everlasting sea,
And I say: this too is the world, this too I sing, this too shall not be forgotten,
For I was there in the black midnight, and I saw, and I remember, and I tell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the manner of "Song of Myself" that describes the grim scene aboard a warship after combat, with piled bodies, a stoic captain, and the surgeon at work.
counterfactuals.output:
**After the Guns Fall Silent**

I am there upon the shattered deck, I do not turn my face away,
I breathe the smoke that hangs like a shroud upon the splintered spars,
I hear the water lapping careless at the wounded hull, indifferent, ancient,
And I say to myself: look, look now, and speak what you have seen.

The bodies are piled where the grape-shot found them, comrade upon comrade,
The young man with his eyes still open toward a sky he cannot see,
The old salt whose hands are curled as if still gripping the halyard,
The powder-boy, no more than a child, laid gentle against the coaming—
I do not step over them, I kneel, I lay my palm upon each brow,
For I contain them, every one, the fallen and the falling.

And there stands the captain, straight as the mainmast that yet holds,
His coat torn open, his cheek streaked black with battle's ink,
He does not weep, he does not tremble, he counts his living and his dead,
Stoic as granite, yet I see the tide behind his eyes,
The sea that will not break upon his face until the watch is done.
He gives his orders low, and the men obey, and the ship swings homeward,
And I love him for the sorrow he will not let the world unlock.

Below, in the red lantern-glow, the surgeon bends to his labor,
His sleeves rolled past the elbow, his arms baptized in the work of mercy,
The saw, the probe, the needle, the swift and terrible tenderness,
He does not flinch at the crying-out, he answers it with steadiness of hand.
Here a leg comes off and is carried away, here a fever is soothed with a word,
The floor is slick and the buckets fill, and still he does not pause—
I honor him, the butcher who is also the saint, the last friend of the maimed.

I am the dying man who grips his wrist and calls him brother,
I am the amputated limb, cast without ceremony to the deep,
I am the captain's silence and the surgeon's aching shoulders,
I am the smoke, the blood, the salt, the groan, the stubborn beating heart.

Do you think this is only death? I tell you it is also the fierce persistence of the living,
The scrubbing of the decks, the mending of the sail, the burial at dawn,
The names spoken once into the wind and given to the waves,
And the ship, wounded, unconquered, moving on across the vast and healing water.

I sound my barbaric witness over the roofs of the ocean—
None of it is lost, none of it forgotten, all of it is folded into me,
And I carry it onward, and I set it down here, that you too may hold it,
For what befell them befalls us all, and I do not look away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a passage of Whitman-esque catalog verse about a midnight sea battle's grisly aftermath, ending with a line about these images being irretrievable.
counterfactuals.output:
**Aftermath at the Midnight Sea**

O the water black as the throat of a bell, and the moon a smear of tallow upon it,
The splintered spars adrift, the shrouds trailing like the hair of drowned women,
The deck slick and steaming, the scuppers running their slow red confession into the brine.

I see them—I do not turn my eyes away:
The gunner slumped against his cold iron, his hands still cupping the powder he will never light,
The boy from the topmast folded impossibly, a broken gull upon the boards,
The surgeon by his lantern sawing, the bucket beside him brimming and overbrimming,
The wounded who call for their mothers in three languages, and the mothers ten thousand miles asleep,
The one who laughs, the one who prays, the one who says nothing and means it forever.

The salt-wind carrying the smell of scorched flesh and tar and the sweetish rot beginning,
The rats already at their industry in the dark hold,
The flag half-burned yet nailed, defiant and idiot, to its blackened staff,
The men bailing, the men weeping, the men too spent for either,
The dead sliding overside with a small sound, a stitch drawn through their canvas, a shot at their feet,
The phosphorescence troubling the wake where they sink, greenish, patient, taking them in.

I stood among them, I breathed that breathing air, I laid my palm on the still-warm iron,
And the sea closed its enormous book upon the whole of it—
And these images I give you now are the last that shall ever be given,
For they are gone into the water that keeps nothing and remembers nothing,
And no man living shall look upon them again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write free verse in the style of 19th-century American poetry cataloging the sights, sounds, and smells of a mortally wounded ship after a night engagement.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wreck Toward Morning**

O the ship!—the shattered ship, the death-listing hull upon the black-glassed sea,
I sing her now, I catalog her wounds while the powder-smoke drifts thinning into stars.

Come, see with me the deck by lantern-shine and the low red coals of the fires not yet drowned:
The splintered mast leaning, its canvas trailing like a broken wing in the water,
The shrouds parted, the rigging hanging in torn nooses,
The great gun overturned, its muzzle cold now, wreathed in curling smoke,
The deck-planks pried and glistening—glistening dark, dark, and I will not name with what.

Hear the sounds, the after-sounds, when the roar has passed and left its ringing:
The creak, the long slow groan of timbers working, working toward their end,
The suck and gurgle of the sea in the wound below the waterline,
The drip—incessant drip—from spar and rope and the surgeon's swinging lamp,
The low talk of the living, the hushed word, the name called softly and not answered,
The one voice singing (why does he sing?) a hymn half-forgotten,
And under all, the pumps—clank, clank—the failing pumps that will not save her.

And now the smells, that I must set down too, for a truthful poem hides nothing:
The bitter sulphur-reek of burnt powder hanging in the shrouds,
The tar, the brine, the wet rope steaming,
The sweet-sick copper smell that clings, that follows down the ladder into the dark,
The charred oak, the scorched sailcloth, the smoke of oil and pitch,
The salt—the everlasting salt—washing it, washing it, and never clean.

She settles. Slowly, slowly she gives herself over.
And I, standing witness in the gray of the coming day,
Take off my cap to her, this mortal ship, this hull of oak and men,
And speak my catalog aloud that she go not unmourned into the swallowing sea—

O ship, O broken sister of the night, I have seen you,
I have heard you, I have breathed the very air of your dying,
And I carry you, I carry you, into the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, unrhymed poem imitating Walt Whitman that lists the horrors of a defeated but victorious ship at night—corpses, flames, guns, stars, and the surgeon's saw.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Ship That Won by Dying**

Come now and see what victory costs, come down into the smoke with me,
For I was there when the guns fell silent and the silence was the worst of all the sounds.

The ship still floats, but she floats like a wounded thing, low in the black water,
Her masts hang splintered, her sails are shrouds, her decks are slick with what men carry inside them.
We have won—hear how the word tastes of iron and salt and burning tar—we have won.

Behold the corpses, my comrades, my brothers, laid out and heaped and tangled,
The young one with his mouth still open as if to finish a word he began at noon,
The old one clutching the ropes, his hands refusing even now to let the ship go down,
Faces I kissed at morning muster, faces now the color of the moon,
They lie along the gunwales, they lie in the scuppers, they roll a little with the swell.

And the flames, see how the flames walk the rigging like curious children,
Licking, climbing, whispering in the canvas, hungry and unhurried and bright,
Casting their red across the water, across the dead, across the living who are half dead too,
Painting the whole wreck in the color of the wound.

The guns are cooling now, the great throats that roared are quiet,
Blackened, smoking, their bronze still warm as flesh, spent and satisfied and terrible,
Their work is finished and their work lies everywhere around them, unburied, unblessed.

Look up—above the smoke the stars are out, indifferent, ancient, clean,
They do not care that we have won, they wheel and shine as they shone before we were born,
They will shine the same when this ship and all her names have rotted to the reef,
And that, I tell you, that indifference of the stars is a horror deeper than the dead.

Below, in the hold, hear the surgeon at his labor,
Hear the saw, the patient saw, going back and forth, back and forth in the lamplight,
Hear the man who does not scream because he has no screaming left in him,
See the pile of limbs beside the table growing, growing, a harvest of the night,
The surgeon's arms are red to the elbow and his eyes are somewhere far away.

This is victory, then. This is the thing we cheered for.
The flag still flies, torn and smoke-stained, nailed to what remains of the mast,
And under it we drift toward morning, we the winners, we the ruined,
Rocked on the dark by the same sea that will take us all in the end,
Singing no song, only listening—to the flames, to the saw, to the vast and silent stars.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
